summaries.example: Imagine a story about a dragon named Nori who lives in a crystal cave. Nori is not a real animal, and the cave is not a real place. Still, the story lets us talk about Nori and the cave. One philosopher might say they exist only in the story. Another might say they are special objects created by storytelling. A third might say they do not exist at all, and that we are only pretending while we tell the story.
summaries.summary: Fictional entities are characters, places, animals, and objects that appear in fiction. Sherlock Holmes is a character, while London is a real place used in the Holmes stories. Philosophy asks what fictional entities would be like and whether they exist at all. Possibilists place them in other possible worlds. Meinongian theories allow objects that do not exist to have story-given properties. Creationist theories treat fictional entities as abstract objects made through storytelling. Antirealist theories deny that fictional entities exist and explain our talk through descriptions, stories, or make-believe. The entry shows that even simple sentences about stories raise difficult questions about existence, identity, and language.
key_ideas: Characters such as Sherlock Holmes and places such as Rivendell are examples of fictional entities.
Philosophers ask two different questions: What are fictional entities like, and are there any fictional entities?
Some theories treat fictional things as possible objects, nonexistent objects with properties, or abstract creations.
Other theories say talk about fictional things can be explained by make-believe without adding fictional objects to reality.
A real person or place can appear in a story without becoming fictional; London may be the setting of a Holmes story, while Holmes is fictional.
summaries.why_it_matters: Stories are important in everyday life, school, art, and culture. We easily say that a character is brave or that a place is imaginary, but these sentences are not as simple as they seem. Thinking about them helps us understand the difference between reality, possibility, imagination, and pretending. It also shows how philosophers compare different explanations instead of quickly choosing one.

important_terms.definition: A person, animal, place, or thing that appears in a story but is not part of the real world as described by the story.
The question of what a fictional thing would be like if there were such things.
The question of whether fictional things exist at all.
A view that says fictional things do not exist in the real world, but might exist in other possible worlds.
A view that says some objects can have properties even though they do not exist.
A view that says authors make fictional objects through storytelling and related practices.

questions_to_think_about: When you say “the dragon is green,” are you saying something about the real world or about the story?
Can something have properties, such as being golden or round, without existing?
Does writing a story create a new kind of thing?
Why might a real place in a story be different from a fictional place?

summaries.example: Suppose two writers independently produce word-for-word identical stories about a detective named Mira. A theory that identifies a fictional character only with the properties described in a story may seem to predict one Mira, since the descriptions match. Yet it is natural to say there are two characters: one created in each work. This pressures a neo-Meinongian theory, which emphasizes characterizing properties, and supports the creationist insight that the history of storytelling may matter to identity. Creationism, however, faces its own questions: how exactly is a character created, and how many indistinguishable fictional characters does one story contain?
summaries.summary: The entry separates two debates. The metaphysical debate asks what fictional entities would be if there were any. The ontological debate asks whether there are fictional entities in the first place. Possibilism treats Holmes-like characters as inhabitants of nonactual worlds, but it struggles to determine which of many matching individuals is Holmes and to explain why fictional properties matter in actual comparisons and attitudes. Meinongian approaches allow nonexistent objects to have characterizing properties. Concrete neo-Meinongianism treats them as concrete correlates of property collections, while abstract neo-Meinongianism treats them more like abstract roles or property-bearing objects. A related dispute concerns special kinds of properties versus special modes of predication, such as encoding and exemplifying. Creationism instead makes fictional entities abstract artifacts generated through authorial or cultural practices, giving storytelling a central role but facing problems about intention, generation, persistence, and identity. At the ontological level, realists defend fictional entities, while antirealists use Russellian paraphrase, intensional “according to the fiction” approaches, or pretense theory. Quantified talk about fictional entities and arguments from fictional works may support realism, but critics argue that similar language can describe imaginary or mistaken objects without committing us to them. The entry presents these positions as an unsettled philosophical dispute.
key_ideas: The metaphysical question asks what fictional entities would be like; the ontological question asks whether there are any.
Possibilism faces an individuation problem: several possible individuals may fit everything a story says about Holmes, and it is unclear which one is Holmes.
Meinongian theories explain how Holmes can be clever or a detective in the story-given sense even though he lacks ordinary existence.
Neo-Meinongians disagree about whether fictional objects are concrete correlates of properties or abstract objects that encode properties.
They also disagree about whether fictional objects have special kinds of properties or possess ordinary properties in a special mode, such as encoding rather than exemplifying.

Creationism explains why authors and storytelling seem important, but it must clarify the creative process and the identity of the objects created; antirealists challenge the need for such objects at all.
summaries.why_it_matters: Fiction appears to involve reference, truth, properties, and identity, even when its characters and settings are not ordinary real objects. The debate therefore connects metaphysics with logic, semantics, literary interpretation, and the philosophy of language. It also tests a general philosophical question: should what our language seems to say determine what exists, or should language be explained by a deeper theory of reality and social practice? Comparing realist and antirealist accounts helps readers see why apparently ordinary claims can support competing theories.

important_terms.definition: The position that fictional entities exist in some sense; fictional antirealism denies that there are any such entities.
A theory locating fictional entities in nonactual possible worlds rather than the actual world.
A family of views holding that objects may lack existence while still having properties in terms of which they are characterized.
The claim that an object has the properties used to characterize it, whether or not it exists.
A neo-Meinongian view that treats nonexistent objects characterized by physical properties as concrete correlates of property sets.
A neo-Meinongian view that treats such objects as abstract objects, roles, or something like Platonic attributes.
The view that fictional entities are abstract artifacts dependent on authors, works, or practices of make-believe.
An antirealist approach explaining fictional discourse through contexts of imagining or pretending rather than genuine reference.

questions_to_think_about: If two stories describe indistinguishable characters, should there be one fictional character or two? Why?
Does the truth of “Holmes is a detective” differ from the truth of “Holmes is a fictional character”?
Can a theory explain both the properties a story gives a character and the character’s dependence on storytelling?
Do true sentences that quantify over fictional characters prove that fictional entities exist?
What would count as an ontological argument, rather than merely a useful way of speaking?

summaries.example: Consider a school play about a detective named Jo. During the play, a student says, “Jo solved the mystery.” Inside the story, this is true. Afterward, another student says, “Jo is a fictional character.” This is also true in an ordinary conversation, but it means something different. The first sentence describes what happens in the play; the second describes Jo’s status outside the play. A philosopher must explain how both sentences can be meaningful without simply treating Jo as an ordinary real person.
summaries.summary: Fictional entities are the characters, places, and objects presented in works of fiction. The entry distinguishes the metaphysical question—what such entities would be like—from the ontological question—whether any exist. Possibilism says they exist only in other possible worlds, but several possible individuals may satisfy the same story, creating a problem about which one is the character. Meinongian theories take fictional objects to lack ordinary existence while still having properties supplied by their descriptions. Neo-Meinongian versions differ over whether these objects are concrete correlates of properties or abstract objects resembling roles, and they debate whether fictional objects have special properties or possess familiar properties in a special way. Creationism says fictional entities are abstract artifacts dependent on authors, works, or practices of make-believe. It captures the idea that storytelling brings characters into being, but it must explain exactly when creation occurs and how characters are identified. Fictional realists accept fictional entities, while antirealists seek explanations that do not. Russellian paraphrase, “according to the story” constructions, and pretense theory are attempts to explain why fictional sentences can seem true without requiring fictional objects. Realists reply that some claims about fictional characters, especially quantified claims, may resist such explanations. The entry concludes that neither side has an easy victory.
key_ideas: Fictional entities include not only characters such as Holmes but also fictional places and objects. Real places and people may serve as settings or subjects without being fictional entities.
Possibilism compares fictional entities with merely possible objects, but it must explain why many possible individuals can fit the same fictional description.
Meinongian views preserve the intuition that a character really is clever or brave in the way the story presents the character, even while denying ordinary existence.
Creationism explains the apparent role of authors by making fictional entities dependent abstract artifacts, though the details of creation and identity remain controversial.
At the level of language, antirealists try to paraphrase fictional claims or explain them through make-believe; realists argue that some external claims resist those paraphrases.
The source distinguishes sentences true within a story from sentences about a story or its characters in the actual world.
summaries.why_it_matters: We constantly move between talking inside a story and talking about a story. Understanding that difference clarifies how language can be meaningful even when its names do not refer to ordinary real things. The debate also introduces major philosophical tools: possible worlds, descriptions, quantifiers, properties, identity, and make-believe. It shows why philosophers examine both the structure of sentences and the kinds of entities that a theory says the world contains.

important_terms.definition: A character, setting, or object presented by a work of fiction, rather than an ordinary entity in the real world.
A philosophical position that says fictional entities exist in some sense.
A philosophical position that says there are no fictional entities, even though fictional discourse is meaningful.
The question of what kind of thing a fictional entity would be if fictional entities exist.
The question of whether fictional entities exist at all.
The theory that fictional entities exist in other possible worlds, not in the actual world.
The family of theories associated with the idea that nonexistent objects can still be characterized as having properties.
The theory that fictional entities are abstract artifacts brought about through storytelling or related practices.

questions_to_think_about: Why might “Jo solved the mystery” and “Jo is fictional” require different kinds of explanation?
Would a possible Jo be the same as the fictional Jo? What might make them different?
Does an author’s intention create a character, or is a written work and a shared practice also needed?
Can we talk truly about a fictional character without believing that the character exists?
Why might two independently written stories with identical descriptions contain two characters rather than one?
